comp.label: In Defence of Mistakes
comp.compStory:
Somewhere in your house, there is probably a rubber. It may be small and grubby, worn down to a nub, with a pencil point stabbed into it during a long and difficult lesson. It is not an exciting object. Nobody has ever asked for one as a birthday present. And yet it may be one of the most honest things you own, because it exists for one reason only: everybody makes mistakes.

We do not always behave as though we believe this. In many classrooms, a cross in the margin feels like a small defeat. A wrong answer said out loud can turn a face red for the rest of the morning. We learn, very early, that being right earns praise and being wrong earns, at best, a sympathetic look. So we start to protect ourselves. We put our hands up only when we are certain. We choose the easy question instead of the interesting one. We stop trying things we might not be good at.

This essay is an argument that we have got it the wrong way round. Mistakes are not the opposite of learning. Very often, they are where learning begins.

Think about how you learned to ride a bike, if you have. Nobody handed you a set of instructions and expected a perfect ride on the first attempt. You wobbled. You fell off. You put a foot down too early, then too late, then at roughly the right moment. Each wobble told your body something that no instruction could: lean a little less, pedal a little faster, look ahead instead of down. If you had refused to wobble, you would still be standing beside the bike, perfectly upright and going nowhere.

The same is true of almost everything worth learning. A wrong answer in a maths problem is not just a wrong answer. It is a clue. It shows exactly where your thinking took a turn it should not have, and that is far more useful than a lucky guess that happened to be right. A teacher who looks carefully at your mistakes can learn more about how your mind works than one who only counts your ticks.

Of course, not every mistake is welcome. Nobody wants a pilot who is "learning from mistakes" during a landing, or a surgeon who is "just having a go". Some situations demand that we get things right first time, and in those situations people practise for years, often making their mistakes somewhere safe, so that they do not make them where it matters. But notice what that means: even the experts we trust the most became expert by getting things wrong, many times, in the right places.

Perhaps the real problem is not mistakes themselves but how we feel about them. If a mistake makes us feel stupid, we hide it, and a hidden mistake teaches nothing. If we can treat it instead as information, as a signpost saying "not this way", then it becomes something we can use. The difference is not in the mistake. It is in us. People who invent, discover or create things tend to know this well. Their notebooks are full of crossings-out, false starts and ideas that did not work, and those messy pages are often the most interesting ones to read.

There is a kind of courage involved in this. It takes courage to say, "I don't understand," in front of other people. It takes courage to attempt the harder question, knowing that you might fail. But that courage is catching. When one person admits they are stuck, others often discover they were stuck too, and the whole room learns something. A classroom where mistakes are allowed is not a careless classroom. It is a brave one.

So here is a modest proposal. The next time you get something wrong, before you reach for the rubber, pause for a moment. Ask yourself what the mistake is trying to tell you. Then rub it out, by all means, and try again.

Just do not rub out the lesson along with it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer begin the essay by describing a rubber?
questions.optionA: To explain how rubbers are made
questions.optionB: To suggest that rubbers should be banned
questions.optionC: To advertise a new kind of rubber
questions.optionD: To complain about untidy pencil cases
questions.optionE: To use an everyday object to show that everybody makes mistakes
questions.explanation: A rubber 'exists for one reason only: everybody makes mistakes', which sets up the whole argument.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The writer calls the rubber "one of the most honest things you own". What does this mean?
questions.optionA: It was cheap to buy
questions.optionB: It never breaks
questions.optionC: It is always telling the truth about spelling
questions.optionE: It openly admits that mistakes are normal
questions.explanation: Its very existence admits that people get things wrong.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: According to the second paragraph, which of these do people do to protect themselves?
questions.optionA: Ride a bike without falling off
questions.optionB: Ask for a rubber as a present
questions.optionC: Practise for years somewhere safe
questions.optionE: Put their hands up only when they are certain
questions.explanation: 'We put our hands up only when we are certain.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What does the writer mean by "we have got it the wrong way round"?
questions.optionA: We write our answers in the wrong order
questions.optionB: We give praise to the wrong people
questions.optionC: We should learn to ride bikes backwards
questions.optionD: We hold our pencils upside down
questions.optionE: We treat mistakes as the enemy of learning when they are often the start of it
questions.explanation: The next sentences explain: 'Mistakes are not the opposite of learning... they are where learning begins.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer use the example of learning to ride a bike?
questions.optionA: Because cycling is the writer's favourite hobby
questions.optionB: Because it is a lesson taught in schools
questions.optionC: Because it shows that instructions are always useful
questions.optionE: Because most readers will remember that they could only learn it by wobbling and falling
questions.explanation: It is a familiar experience in which mistakes clearly taught something no instructions could.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "perfectly upright and going nowhere". What point does this phrase make?
questions.optionA: Good posture is important
questions.optionB: Standing still is the safest way to ride a bike
questions.optionC: The bike was broken
questions.optionD: Avoiding mistakes completely would also mean never making progress
questions.optionE: The rider was too tired to move
questions.explanation: You would avoid falling but also never move: no mistakes, but no learning either.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Which word is closest in meaning to "sympathetic" as used in the essay?
questions.optionA: amused
questions.optionB: angry
questions.optionC: kind and understanding
questions.optionE: proud
questions.explanation: A sympathetic look shows someone feels sorry for you and understands.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: According to the writer, why is a wrong answer in maths "a clue"?
questions.optionA: It shows exactly where your thinking went wrong
questions.optionB: It is always nearly right
questions.optionC: It can be rubbed out easily
questions.optionE: It tells the teacher you were not trying
questions.explanation: 'It shows exactly where your thinking took a turn it should not have.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How does the writer feel about lucky guesses?
questions.optionA: They are a kind of cheating
questions.optionB: They are the best way to learn
questions.optionC: They show that the pupil is clever
questions.optionD: They should be rewarded with extra ticks
questions.optionE: They are less useful than a wrong answer that shows how you were thinking
questions.explanation: A mistake is 'far more useful than a lucky guess that happened to be right'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer include the paragraph about pilots and surgeons?
questions.optionA: To change the subject completely
questions.optionB: To show that pilots and surgeons are careless
questions.optionC: To admit that some mistakes are not acceptable, which makes the argument more balanced
questions.optionD: To suggest that readers should become surgeons
questions.optionE: To prove that mistakes are always dangerous
questions.explanation: 'Of course, not every mistake is welcome' answers an obvious objection before a reader can raise it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What does the writer suggest experts do so that they do not make mistakes where it matters?
questions.optionA: Practise a great deal and make their mistakes somewhere safe
questions.optionB: Ask somebody else to do the difficult parts
questions.optionC: Avoid all difficult situations
questions.optionE: Never practise in case they get things wrong
questions.explanation: 'People practise for years, often making their mistakes somewhere safe.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "a hidden mistake teaches nothing". Why might this be true?
questions.optionA: Because only spoken mistakes count
questions.optionB: Because teachers cannot mark them
questions.optionC: If nobody looks at the mistake, nobody can learn what caused it
questions.optionE: Because hidden mistakes disappear by themselves
questions.explanation: To learn from a mistake you have to examine it; hiding it removes that chance.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The writer describes a mistake as "a signpost saying 'not this way'". What does this metaphor suggest?
questions.optionA: Mistakes are found by the side of roads
questions.optionB: You should ignore mistakes and carry on
questions.optionC: A mistake can guide you towards the right path
questions.optionD: Mistakes are written in large letters
questions.optionE: You should always turn back when you are lost
questions.explanation: A signpost directs travellers; a mistake points you away from a wrong route.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The writer says that courage is "catching". What does this mean?
questions.optionA: Courage is a kind of illness
questions.optionB: Courage is easy to lose
questions.optionC: Brave people are good at catching balls
questions.optionD: Only some people can ever be brave
questions.optionE: When one person is brave, others are encouraged to be brave too
questions.explanation: Like a cold spreading, one person admitting they are stuck helps others to admit it too.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What, according to the writer, is a classroom where mistakes are allowed?
questions.optionA: A brave one
questions.optionB: A careless one
questions.optionC: A dangerous one
questions.optionE: An unusual one
questions.explanation: 'A classroom where mistakes are allowed is not a careless classroom. It is a brave one.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer call the suggestion near the end "a modest proposal"?
questions.optionA: To show it is a small, simple step that anyone could take
questions.optionB: To make the idea sound very important
questions.optionC: To ask the reader for money
questions.optionD: To suggest that the idea is old-fashioned
questions.optionE: To show that the writer is not sure it will work
questions.explanation: Pausing before rubbing out is a small, achievable action rather than a big change.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How does the final sentence link back to the start of the essay?
questions.optionA: It describes buying a new rubber
questions.optionB: It introduces a new argument about pencils
questions.optionC: It disagrees with the opening paragraph
questions.optionD: It lists all the writer's own mistakes
questions.optionE: It returns to the rubber, warning us not to erase what the mistake taught us
questions.explanation: The essay opens and closes with the rubber, ending on the idea of keeping the lesson.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What is the main purpose of the essay?
questions.optionA: To argue that tests should be harder
questions.optionB: To describe a day in a classroom
questions.optionC: To teach readers how to ride a bike
questions.optionD: To persuade readers to see mistakes as a useful part of learning
questions.optionE: To explain how surgeons are trained
questions.explanation: Every paragraph supports the claim that mistakes, treated well, help us learn.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 2,856 ÷ 12?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 3/4 ÷ 3/8?
questions.explanation: Dividing by 3/8 is multiplying by 8/3: 3/4 × 8/3 = 24/12 = 2.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest:
Which of these fractions is the largest?
2/5   3/7   4/9   1/2   5/9
questions.explanation: 5/9 is the only one greater than 1/2; the others are all less than a half.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A school trip has 60 places and 45 have been booked. What percentage has been booked?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Lily saves £30. Each year she earns 4% of £30 in interest. How much interest does she earn in 3 years?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: In a class the ratio of boys to girls is 2 : 5. There are 35 children. How many more girls than boys are there?
questions.explanation: 7 parts = 35, so one part is 5. Boys 10, girls 25: 25 − 10 = 15.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: If p = 3 and q = 4, what is 2(p + q)²?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the 15th term of the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …?
questions.explanation: The terms are the square numbers, so the 15th is 15² = 225.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: For the numbers 12, 9, 6, 14 and 9, which statement is true?
questions.optionA: The median is 6
questions.optionB: The mode is 14
questions.optionC: The mean is 9
questions.optionD: The median and the mode are both 9
questions.optionE: The range is 6
questions.explanation: In order: 6, 9, 9, 12, 14. Median 9, mode 9, range 8, mean 50 ÷ 5 = 10.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Two equal circles fit exactly inside a rectangle 16 cm long, touching each other and the sides. What is the radius of each circle?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A cuboid is 9 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm tall. What is its total surface area?
questions.optionA: 15 cm²
questions.optionB: 124 cm²
questions.optionC: 72 cm²
questions.optionE: 144 cm²

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are each 65°. What is the top angle?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A sack holds 2.5 kg of rice. How many 250 g portions can be made from it?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: School starts at 08:15. There are three lessons of 50 minutes, with a 10-minute break after the first and after the second. When does the third lesson end?
questions.explanation: 3 × 50 = 150 min and 2 × 10 = 20 min: 170 min = 2 h 50 min after 08:15, which is 11:05.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the lowest common multiple of 6 and 8?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24 … and 24 is the first that 6 also divides.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is −3 − (−8)?
questions.explanation: Taking away a negative is the same as adding: −3 + 8 = 5.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
questions.explanation: A regular hexagon has 3 lines through opposite corners and 3 through the middles of opposite sides.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A coin is tossed and a fair dice is rolled. What is the probability of getting a head and a 6?
questions.explanation: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. (There are 12 equally likely outcomes and only one is head-and-6.)

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Pens cost n pence and pencils cost 2p more than pens. Five pens and three pencils cost 70p. How much is a pen?
questions.optionA: 7p
questions.optionB: 8p
questions.optionC: 6p

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, GARDEN is written as AGDRNE. How would PLANET be written in the same code?
questions.optionA: LPNATE
questions.optionB: TENALP
questions.optionC: LPANTE
questions.optionE: LNPATE
questions.explanation: The letters are swapped in pairs: PL→LP, AN→NA, ET→TE.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, BREAD is written as CS21E. How would GHOST be written in the same code?
questions.optionA: HI4UV
questions.optionB: GH4ST
questions.optionC: HI4TU
questions.optionE: FG4RS
questions.explanation: Vowels become numbers (A=1, E=2, I=3, O=4, U=5) and every consonant moves forward one letter: G→H, H→I, O→4, S→T, T→U.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next letter: B, D, G, K, P, ?
questions.optionA: X
questions.optionB: V
questions.optionC: U
questions.optionE: T
questions.explanation: The gaps grow by one: +2, +3, +4, +5, so next is +6: P → V.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 2, 12, 30, 56, ?
questions.explanation: The differences are 10, 18, 26, going up by 8, so next is 34: 56 + 34 = 90.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 50, 2, 45, 4, 40, 8, ?
questions.explanation: Two series take turns: 50, 45, 40, 35 goes down by 5; 2, 4, 8 doubles. Next is 35.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
The numbers in each group are related in the same way. Find the missing number.
8 (6) 4     10 (7) 4     20 ( ? ) 6
questions.explanation: The middle number is halfway between the outside numbers: (20 + 6) ÷ 2 = 13.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Which letter ends the first word and starts the second word in BOTH pairs?
fla ( ? ) ime        bea ( ? ) ide
questions.optionA: n
questions.optionB: w
questions.optionC: p
questions.optionE: t
questions.explanation: flat, time and beat, tide. No other letter makes four real words.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three letters that make a word have been taken out of the word in capitals. Which three letters complete it?
The WHER was warm and sunny all week.
questions.optionA: EAT
questions.optionB: ITS
questions.optionC: ARE
questions.optionE: AIL
questions.explanation: W + EAT + HER = WEATHER.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word can go in front of all of these to make three new words?  ___print   ___step   ___ball
questions.optionA: finger
questions.optionB: door
questions.optionC: hand
questions.optionE: foot
questions.explanation: footprint, footstep, football. Each of the others fails with at least one.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of TRANQUIL?
questions.optionA: distant
questions.optionB: gentle
questions.optionC: silent
questions.optionE: peaceful
questions.explanation: Tranquil means calm; agitated means troubled and restless.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is closest in meaning to DILIGENT?
questions.optionA: quick
questions.optionB: hard-working
questions.optionC: lazy
questions.optionE: polite
questions.explanation: Diligent means showing care and effort in your work.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three of these words go together. Which TWO do not belong?
kitten   puppy   calf   mare   ewe
questions.optionA: calf, ewe
questions.optionB: puppy, mare
questions.optionC: kitten, calf
questions.optionE: kitten, puppy
questions.explanation: Kitten, puppy and calf are young animals. A mare and a ewe are adult females.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Three houses stand in a row: one red, one blue and one green. The green house is immediately to the right of the blue house. The red house is not on the right. Which colour is the house on the left?
questions.optionA: It could be blue or red
questions.optionB: red
questions.optionC: It cannot be worked out
questions.optionE: blue
questions.explanation: Blue and green must be next to each other, in houses 1–2 or 2–3. If they were 1–2, red would be on the right, which is not allowed. So blue and green are 2 and 3, and red is on the left.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Yesterday was the day before Monday. What day will it be in 10 days' time?
questions.optionA: Friday
questions.optionB: Sunday
questions.optionC: Thursday
questions.optionE: Wednesday
questions.explanation: Yesterday was Sunday, so today is Monday. 10 days = 1 week + 3 days: Thursday.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Rearrange the letters in capitals to make a word that completes the sentence sensibly.
The robin built its SETN in the hedge.
questions.optionA: nets
questions.optionB: sent
questions.optionC: stem
questions.optionE: tens
questions.explanation: SETN can make NEST, TENS, SENT or NETS, but only a NEST makes sense.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word can NOT be made using only the letters of THUNDERSTORM? (Each letter may be used only as many times as it appears.)
questions.optionA: hunters
questions.optionB: thunder
questions.optionC: trumpet
questions.optionE: monster
questions.explanation: THUNDERSTORM has no P, so TRUMPET cannot be made.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Doctor is to hospital as chef is to ?
questions.optionA: cook
questions.optionB: kitchen
questions.optionC: apron
questions.optionE: food
questions.explanation: A doctor works in a hospital; a chef works in a kitchen.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Change one letter at a time to turn BEAR into BOAT. Which word could go in the middle?
BEAR → ? → BOAT
questions.optionA: BRAT
questions.optionB: BEAD
questions.optionC: BEAK
questions.optionE: BEAT
questions.explanation: BEAR → BEAT (R to T) → BOAT (E to O).

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Find the number that completes the third pair in the same way as the first two.
(3 → 10)   (5 → 26)   (7 → ?)
questions.explanation: Square the number and add 1: 9 + 1, 25 + 1, 49 + 1 = 50.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Sam walks 3 km north, turns right and walks 2 km, then turns right again and walks 3 km. In which direction is he now from where he started?
questions.optionA: East
questions.optionB: North-east
questions.optionC: West
questions.optionE: North
questions.explanation: North 3, then east 2, then south 3 brings him back level with the start, 2 km to the east.
